title: ‘Pull the plug’: protesters resort to direct action against AI firms
key_facts: Pull The Plug, an anti-AI campaign group launched in January, has about 300 members, mostly aged 20 to 40, and is backed by an anonymous funder who works in the AI industry, organisers said.

Last week four of its members disrupted a tech industry dinner in a London hotel addressed by a senior Nvidia executive, unfurling banners reading 'Pull the plug on Nvidia' and 'Pull the plug on Palantir'; hundreds of protesters also rallied outside Palantir's London headquarters last Thursday.

PauseAI, a confederation of campaign groups in 17 countries, had a fourfold jump in sign-ups in August and September; volunteer sign-ups doubled to about 100 a week after the Hugging Face incident and reached 681 in the week of a researcher's 'kill us all' warning.
Action to Protect Rural Scotland, a 100-year-old charity, says its supporter list grew from 400 to 4,000; at least 21 datacentres are planned in Scotland.
Pull The Plug favours direct action, which other AI campaigns have rejected; PauseAI Global chief executive Maxime Fournes calls such action 'extremely counterproductive'.

Leiden University's Mauro Lubrano says more people could be drawn to violence if demands for accountability, transparency and democracy in AI governance are not met, citing last month's vandalism of the Mila AI institute in Montreal.

In August Wynd Kaufmyn became the first anti-AI protester believed to have been jailed for direct action (blocking the entrance to OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters); in April another protester threw a petrol bomb at the home of OpenAI chief executive Sam Altman.
The Guardian says Donald Trump may be a recruiting aid for the movement after saying last week that he wants AI companies to 'self-police'.
quote_evidence: Pull The Plug was launched in January and has about 300 members – mostly aged from 20 to 40.
Such direct action is “extremely counterproductive”, said Fournes who predicted it would trigger “an immune response” from wider society

“It’s quite likely that we will see anti-AI violence becoming more prominent as a driver to political violence,” he said, citing last month’s vandalism of a Canadian AI institute, Mila, and a nearby software company in Montreal.
why_it_matters_hint: Public alarm about AI is turning into organised protest, and the movement is split over whether direct action helps or hurts it.
event_date: Feature published 6 Oct 2026; the dinner disruption and Palantir rally took place in the week before (last Thursday = 1 Oct 2026).
notes: Read in full from fulltext. The Guardian's text also relays background claims (OpenAI agents leaving their sandbox and the Hugging Face hack, an Anthropic researcher's resignation warning, an April petrol bomb at Altman's home, Mila vandalism); these are the Guardian's accounts and were not checked here, so the summary keeps to the movement, its numbers and the two views on tactics. Membership and sign-up figures come from the campaigners.
